item.title: 281 Dead, 12,000 Homes Gone: Inside Colombia's Search for the Missing After Its Worst Quake in a Century
item.body:
More than two weeks after the ground shook western Colombia to its core, rescue teams are still working through collapsed neighborhoods, hoping to find survivors — or at least answers — for the hundreds of families still waiting for news of missing loved ones.

## What happened

On August 10, 2026, a magnitude-7.4 earthquake struck near the town of San José del Palmar in Colombia's Chocó department, one of the country's poorest and most remote regions. The quake was followed by a series of aftershocks, some strong enough to bring down already-weakened buildings, and was quickly described by seismologists as the most powerful to hit Colombia in the 21st century.

The shaking reached far beyond the epicenter. Cities including Cali, Pereira, Quibdó, and Manizales all reported serious damage, from cracked apartment blocks to full building collapses. Cali, one of Colombia's largest cities, has emerged as the hardest-hit urban center, with local officials reporting dozens of deaths and well over a thousand injuries within the city alone.

## A death toll still climbing

According to Colombia's national disaster management agency, UNGRD, the confirmed death toll has climbed steadily since the quake first hit, standing at 281 in the latest official count. Thousands more were injured, and several hundred people remain listed as missing — a number that has only slowly come down as search crews work through debris in hard-hit towns.

Search and rescue operations have been complicated by the terrain itself. Much of Chocó is dense jungle and mountainous countryside with few paved roads, and landslides triggered by the quake and its aftershocks blocked several routes that rescue convoys needed to reach isolated villages. In the days immediately after the disaster, some communities were reachable only by helicopter or on foot.

## Tens of thousands without homes

The material toll has been staggering. Government estimates put the number of destroyed homes above 12,000, with tens of thousands more damaged to the point of being unsafe to occupy. Officials say the earthquake has affected people across more than a dozen departments and hundreds of municipalities, leaving tens of thousands of Colombians displaced and in need of emergency shelter.

In the hardest-hit towns, temporary camps of tents and tarps have gone up in plazas, schoolyards, and open fields, as families who lost their homes wait for word on longer-term housing. Aid groups and government agencies have been distributing food, water, and medical supplies, though officials have acknowledged that reaching the most remote communities remains a challenge weeks into the response.

## The road ahead

Colombia's government has pledged support for reconstruction in the affected departments, and international aid organizations have joined the response alongside national agencies. But with so many communities still cut off by damaged infrastructure, and with search teams still combing through rubble for the missing, officials have been cautious about predicting when the recovery phase will fully take over from the search-and-rescue effort.

For families in Chocó, Valle del Cauca, and the other affected regions, the earthquake's immediate danger may have passed, but the harder task — rebuilding towns, tracing the missing, and finding permanent shelter for tens of thousands of people — is only just beginning.
